facts.statement: Angistorhinus is an extinct genus of phytosaur known for its narrow or hook-shaped snout.
facts.quote: Angistorhinus (meaning "narrow snout" or "hook snout") is an extinct genus of phytosaur known from the Late Triassic period of Texas and Wyoming, United States.

facts.statement: The genus was first named by Mehl in 1913, with Angistorhinus grandis designated as the type species.
facts.quote: It was first named by Mehl in 1913 and the type species is Angistorhinus grandis.

facts.statement: Researchers Hungerbühler and Sues hypothesized in 2001 that Angistorhinus is a junior synonym of Rutiodon.
facts.quote: Hungerbühler and Sues (2001) hypothesised that Angistorhinus is a junior synonym of Rutiodon.

facts.statement: In 2010, Michelle R. Stocker retained the validity of both Brachysuchus and A. grandis.
facts.quote: However, in 2010 Michelle R. Stocker retained the validity of Brachysuchus and of A. grandis.

facts.statement: Angistorhinus lived during the Carnian to Norian stages of the Triassic, between 237 and 205.7 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Carnian to Norian (237 to 205.7 million years ago)

facts.statement: Angistorhinus belongs to the subfamily Mystriosuchinae.
Angistorhinus is classified within the family Parasuchidae.
Angistorhinus resembled Parasuchus but had nostrils positioned further back, closer to and above the eyes.
facts.quote: It was similar to Parasuchus but differed in having the nostrils located further back, towards and above the eyes.

facts.statement: Angistorhinus was a massive animal with a skull length of 120–124 cm and an estimated total length of 7 to 8 meters, exceeding the size of any living crocodile.
facts.quote: Angisthorhinus was a huge animal by any standards; the skull length was about 120–124 cm; estimated overall length 7 to 8 meters long, more in A. megalodon, a very large, short and heavy-muzzled form sometimes given its own genus (Brachysuchus), and which far exceeded in size any living crocodile.

facts.statement: Angistorhinus had the lowest enamel thickness relative to crown size among phytosaurs, yet possessed the thickest enamel in absolute terms.
facts.quote: The thickness of the enamel of Angistorhinus was the lowest among phytosaurs relative to overall crown size, although in absolute terms if had the thickest enamel among phytosaurs.

rejected.statement: A possible second species, A. talainti, is known from Triassic deposits in Morocco.
rejected.quote: A possible second species, A. talainti is known from the Triassic of Morocco.
